content.text: A wave is a moving disturbance that propagates through a medium or space. Waves transfer energy and information without transporting the medium as a whole. Mechanical waves require a material medium; electromagnetic waves can travel through vacuum. Matter waves are associated with constituents of matter in quantum mechanics.
equations: c = 299,792,458 m s⁻¹ (speed of electromagnetic waves in vacuum)

content.text: Mechanical waves depend on the elastic properties and inertia of a medium. Oscillation of one constituent affects neighbouring constituents through restoring forces, allowing the disturbance to propagate while particles oscillate about equilibrium positions.

A transverse wave is one in which particles of the medium oscillate perpendicular to the direction of propagation. Such waves require a medium capable of sustaining shear stress, such as a solid or a stretched string.

A longitudinal wave is one in which particles oscillate parallel to the direction of propagation. Sound in air travels as compressions and rarefactions. Longitudinal waves can propagate in solids, liquids and gases because these media can sustain compressive strain.

Progressive or travelling waves carry a disturbance from one part of a medium to another. The medium as a whole does not travel with the wave. At a fixed instant the wave describes a spatial pattern; at a fixed location it describes oscillation over time.

Surface water waves involve a combination of transverse and longitudinal particle motion. Capillary waves have short wavelengths and are restored mainly by surface tension; gravity waves have longer wavelengths and are restored mainly by gravity.
A sinusoidal transverse wave travelling in the positive x direction can be represented by displacement as a function of position and time. The sign in the phase determines the direction of travel.
equations: y(x,t) = a sin(kx + ωt + φ) (negative x direction)
y = A sin(kx − ωt) + B cos(kx − ωt)

content.text: Amplitude a is the maximum displacement from equilibrium and is taken as positive. The phase is kx − ωt + φ and determines displacement at a given position and time. φ is the initial phase angle.
Wavelength λ is the minimum distance between two points in the same phase, such as consecutive crests. Angular wave number k is 2π divided by wavelength.
The period T is the time for one complete oscillation. Frequency ν is the number of oscillations per second; angular frequency ω is related to period and frequency.
For a longitudinal wave, the displacement of an element along the direction of propagation can be represented by s(x,t). The other wave parameters retain the same meanings as in a transverse wave.
The speed of a progressive wave is the speed of a fixed-phase point. It is related to wavelength, frequency, period, angular frequency and angular wave number.
For a stretched string, the wave speed depends on the string tension and its linear mass density. The linear mass density is the mass per unit length.

content.text: For a longitudinal wave in a medium, speed depends on the relevant elastic modulus and density. In a fluid the relevant modulus is the bulk modulus; in a thin linear solid bar the relevant modulus is Young's modulus.
equations: v = √(Y/ρ) (longitudinal wave in a solid bar)

content.text: Newton treated the pressure changes in sound propagation as isothermal. This gives the bulk modulus equal to pressure and predicts a speed lower than the measured value for air.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Speed of sound in an ideal gas: Newton's formula

content.text: Sound pressure variations are sufficiently rapid that they are approximately adiabatic rather than isothermal. For an ideal gas, the adiabatic bulk modulus is γP, where γ = Cp/Cv. This correction gives the experimentally consistent estimate for sound speed in air.

metadata.topic: Laplace correction and speed of sound in gas

content.text: When two or more wave disturbances overlap, the resultant displacement is the algebraic sum of the individual displacements. Each pulse continues to propagate as though the others were absent. Superposition underlies interference.

Two waves of equal amplitude and frequency travelling in the same direction combine to form a harmonic wave whose amplitude depends on their phase difference. In-phase waves interfere constructively; waves differing in phase by π interfere destructively.
equations: φ = π: resultant displacement is zero

content.text: At a rigid boundary or closed end, a reflected pulse undergoes a phase change of π. At a free or open boundary, reflection occurs without phase change, assuming no energy dissipation.
equations: Open boundary: yᵣ = a sin(kx − ωt)

content.text: Standing or stationary waves result from superposition of waves with the same amplitude and wavelength travelling in opposite directions. Their pattern does not travel; different points oscillate with amplitudes that depend on position.
Nodes are fixed points of zero displacement; antinodes are points of maximum amplitude. The distance between consecutive nodes, or consecutive antinodes, is λ/2.

For a string of length L fixed at both ends, both ends are nodes. The boundary conditions restrict the allowed wavelengths and frequencies to discrete normal modes. The lowest frequency is the fundamental or first harmonic.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Normal modes of a string fixed at both ends

content.text: For a pipe open at both ends, each end is a displacement antinode. All harmonics are possible, with the fundamental frequency v/(2L).

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Normal modes of an open pipe

content.text: For a pipe closed at one end and open at the other, the closed end is a displacement node and the open end an antinode. Only odd harmonics occur; the fundamental frequency is v/(4L).

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Normal modes of a pipe closed at one end

content.text: Strings and air columns have particular natural frequencies or normal modes set by their boundary conditions. When an external driving frequency is close to a natural frequency, the system shows resonance.

Beats arise when two sound waves with close but unequal frequencies and comparable amplitudes are superposed. The resultant sound has a rapidly oscillating carrier with an amplitude that waxes and wanes. Beat frequency equals the absolute difference of the two frequencies.

The textbook describes musical pillars at the Nellaiappar temple in Tamil Nadu. Their vibrations depend on the elasticity, density and shape of the stone; the pillars can produce notes or rhythmic beats when tapped.

Mechanical waves require a material medium. Transverse particle motion is perpendicular to propagation; longitudinal motion is parallel. Progressive waves transport energy, and their speed is determined by the medium's elastic and inertial properties.
Key relations for sinusoidal waves include the wave function, wavelength and wave number, period and frequency, wave speed, and the speed of waves on strings and in fluids/gases.

The superposition principle gives the resultant displacement of overlapping waves. Interference may be constructive or destructive. Standing waves have nodes and antinodes, and only specific normal-mode frequencies satisfy the system's boundary conditions.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Chapter summary: interference and standing waves

content.text: A wave is not motion of matter as a whole. Energy, rather than the medium itself, is transferred from one point to another. In mechanical waves, elastic forces couple neighbouring oscillating parts of the medium.
For an observer at rest in a medium, mechanical-wave speed depends on the elastic and other properties of the medium, such as mass density, and not on the velocity of the source.

content.text: A string of mass 2.50 kg is under a tension of 200 N. The length of the stretched string is 20.0 m. If the transverse jerk is struck at one end of the string, how long does the disturbance take to reach the other end?

A stone dropped from the top of a tower of height 300 m splashes into the water of a pond near the base of the tower. When is the splash heard at the top given that the speed of sound in air is 340 m s–1 ? (g = 9.8 m s–2)

A steel wire has a length of 12.0 m and a mass of 2.10 kg. What should be the tension in the wire so that speed of a transverse wave on the wire equals the speed of sound in dry air at 20 °C = 343 m s–1.
Use the formula v P = γ ρ to explain why the speed of sound in air (a) is independent of pressure, (b) increases with temperature, (c) increases with humidity. Reprint 2026-27 PHYSICS 298

You have learnt that a travelling wave in one dimension is represented by a function y = f (x, t) where x and t must appear in the combination x – v t or x + v t, i.e. y = f (x ± v t). Is the converse true? Examine if the following functions for y can possibly represent a travelling wave : (a) (x – vt )2 (b) log [(x + vt)/x0] (c) 1/(x + vt)

A bat emits ultrasonic sound of frequency 1000 kHz in air. If the sound meets a water surface, what is the wavelength of (a) the reflected sound, (b) the transmitted sound? Speed of sound in air is 340 m s –1 and in water 1486 m s–1.

A hospital uses an ultrasonic scanner to locate tumours in a tissue. What is the wavelength of sound in the tissue in which the speed of sound is 1.7 km s–1 ? The operating frequency of the scanner is 4.2 MHz.

A transverse harmonic wave on a string is described by y(x, t) = 3.0 sin (36 t + 0.018 x + π/4) where x and y are in cm and t in s. The positive direction of x is from left to right. (a) Is this a travelling wave or a stationary wave ? If it is travelling, what are the speed and direction of its propagation ? (b) What are its amplitude and frequency ? (c) What is the initial phase at the origin ? (d) What is the least distance between two successive crests in the wave ?

For the wave described in Exercise 14.8, plot the displacement (y) versus (t) graphs for x = 0, 2 and 4 cm. What are the shapes of these graphs? In which aspects does the oscillatory motion in travelling wave differ from one point to another: amplitude, frequency or phase ?

For the travelling harmonic wave y(x, t) = 2.0 cos 2π (10t – 0.0080 x + 0.35) where x and y are in cm and t in s. Calculate the phase difference between oscillatory motion of two points separated by a distance of (a) 4 m, (b) 0.5 m, (c) λ/2, (d) 3λ/4

The transverse displacement of a string (clamped at its both ends) is given by y(x, t) = 0.06 sin 2 3 π x     cos (120 πt) where x and y are in m and t in s. The length of the string is 1.5 m and its mass is 3.0 ×10–2 kg. Answer the following : (a) Does the function represent a travelling wave or a stationary wave? (b) Interpret the wave as a superposition of two waves travelling in opposite directions. What is the wavelength, frequency, and speed of each wave ? Reprint 2026-27 WAVES 299 (c) Determine the tension in the string.

(i) For the wave on a string described in Exercise 15.11, do all the points on the string oscillate with the same (a) frequency, (b) phase, (c) amplitude? Explain your answers. (ii) What is the amplitude of a point 0.375 m away from one end?

Given below are some functions of x and t to represent the displacement (transverse or longitudinal) of an elastic wave. State which of these represent (i) a travelling wave, (ii) a stationary wave or (iii) none at all: (a) y = 2 cos (3x) sin (10t) (b) y x vt = − 2 (c) y = 3 sin (5x – 0.5t) + 4 cos (5x – 0.5t) (d) y = cos x sin t + cos 2x sin 2t

A wire stretched between two rigid supports vibrates in its fundamental mode with a frequency of 45 Hz. The mass of the wire is 3.5 × 10–2 kg and its linear mass density is 4.0 × 10–2 kg m–1. What is (a) the speed of a transverse wave on the string, and (b) the tension in the string?

A metre-long tube open at one end, with a movable piston at the other end, shows resonance with a fixed frequency source (a tuning fork of frequency 340 Hz) when the tube length is 25.5 cm or 79.3 cm. Estimate the speed of sound in air at the temperature of the experiment. The edge effects may be neglected.
A steel rod 100 cm long is clamped at its middle. The fundamental frequency of longitudinal vibrations of the rod are given to be 2.53 kHz. What is the speed of sound in steel?

A pipe 20 cm long is closed at one end. Which harmonic mode of the pipe is resonantly excited by a 430 Hz source ? Will the same source be in resonance with the pipe if both ends are open? (speed of sound in air is 340 m s–1).

Two sitar strings A and B playing the note ‘Ga’ are slightly out of tune and produce beats of frequency 6 Hz. The tension in the string A is slightly reduced and the beat frequency is found to reduce to 3 Hz. If the original frequency of A is 324 Hz, what is the frequency of B?

Explain why (or how): (a) in a sound wave, a displacement node is a pressure antinode and vice versa, (b) bats can ascertain distances, directions, nature, and sizes of the obstacles without any “eyes”, (c) a violin note and sitar note may have the same frequency, yet we can distinguish between the two notes, (d) solids can support both longitudinal and transverse waves, but only longitudinal waves can propagate in gases, and (e) the shape of a pulse gets distorted during propagation in a dispersive medium.
